strengths: Targets a timely and practical problem: scheduling for augmented (tool-calling) LLM inference, where external-call characteristics (call duration, return length, context-handling policy) genuinely differ from standard text-only serving.

The two-stage design (predictive value estimation at admission plus runtime correction after the API call returns) is a sensible way to handle prediction error, and the anti-starvation term addresses a real fairness concern often ignored in SLO-driven schedulers.

Extensive empirical evaluation: two datasets (Merge, ToolBench), two models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), three hardware configurations (RTX 4090, H800, 2x A100), three workload generators (Poisson, fixed-count, Gamma), plus ablations, SLO-attainment, tail latency (P95 TTFT/TPOT), and a component time breakdown showing <1% predictor overhead.
Ablation (Figure 10) cleanly separates the contribution of dynamic token batching from the two-stage scheduler, and the robustness study under bursty arrivals (Table 6) is a useful addition.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are too weak to support the headline claims. Only vLLM and InferCept (both FCFS-based) are compared end-to-end, yet the paper's own motivation (Section 3.1) shows that even random shuffling recovers much of the goodput loss, implying the enormous 30x gains largely reflect FCFS pathology. Missing baselines include the SJF/length-prediction schedulers the paper itself cites (S3, FastServe, Llumarl, APT-serve [10, 19, 31, 41]), and no 'SJF with predicted output length' or 'random' scheduler is evaluated as a middle ground. Without these, it is impossible to attribute gains to the proposed cost model rather than merely to non-FCFS ordering.

The core scheduling value (Equations 4-25) is an elaborate hand-crafted heuristic, but it is never validated: no sensitivity analysis for the anti-starvation coefficient alpha, the token-limit bounds beta_low/beta_high, gamma, or target_max is provided; the cost model's linearized iteration-time approximations are untested against measured times; and there is no comparison against simpler value functions (e.g., predicted remaining work alone). The design risks being an uninterpretable pile of tuned constants.

The prediction module is under-specified and weakly evaluated. '85% accuracy' for discretized output-length classification is reported without the bucket granularity, without a baseline (e.g., prompt-length-only regression), and without any analysis of how misclassification propagates into scheduling errors - the very failure mode the two-stage design is meant to mitigate. API-call duration prediction (MSE of ~5s) seems large relative to the 1s TTFT SLO but its impact is not analyzed.

Fairness of the vLLM baseline is unclear. vLLM does not natively support pausing/resuming requests across external calls; how it was adapted (apparently discarding KV cache and recomputing) is described only in passing, and this likely handicaps it substantially, inflating relative gains.

Fit and framing for ICML: this is a systems/scheduling paper with a heuristic cost model and a trivial proposition (Proposition 1 is straightforward algebra), little methodological novelty for the ML audience, and no learning component beyond a fine-tuned BERT regressor. Precedent exists (InferCept at ICML'24), but the technical depth here is thinner.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or artifact release is mentioned, key configuration details (SLO settings per experiment, bucket sizes, hyperparameter values) are scattered or deferred, and the merged 'Merge' dataset construction is described too briefly to reconstruct.

No limitations discussion: single-instance serving only (no multi-GPU tensor/disaggregated settings beyond naive 2xA100), no modern models (OPT-13B/GPT-J are dated), no consideration of concurrent/asynchronous tool calls [13], and no discussion of adversarial or non-stationary API latencies.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: serving augmented (tool-calling) LLMs where external calls pause execution, cause HoL blocking, and degrade SLO-satisfying goodput.

Well-motivated design grounded in a formal request-lifecycle model (Eq. 1-3) that explicitly captures multi-stage execution and cross-round state evolution, which distinguishes the approach from per-round SJF heuristics (e.g., MARS).

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-3-70B), GPUs (RTX4090, H800, A100s), two trace datasets, Poisson and bursty (Gamma) arrivals, ablations of both components (Table 2), scheduling overhead analysis (Table 3, 6), prediction-error robustness (Fig. 8), beta sensitivity (Table 5), tail latency, SLO attainment, and memory-occupancy analysis.

Honest treatment of limitations: the theoretical guarantee (Appendix E) is explicitly scoped to a simplified per-iteration knapsack subproblem, and prediction inaccuracy is empirically studied rather than hidden.
Clear writing and a coherent system narrative connecting motivation (Figures 2-5, Table 1) to the two design components (state-aware scheduling, dynamic token budget).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty over prior work: the context-handling policy selection (Preserve/Discard/Swap) and the memory-waste formulation are adopted directly from INFERCEPT (Appendix B explicitly says so), and the scheduler is essentially a cost-weighted, aging-augmented SJF with greedy knapsack packing. The core contribution is a careful combination and integration rather than a new mechanism.

The scheduling value formulation (Eq. 2) is somewhat overstated: the throughput term is a constant '1' that does not differentiate requests, so the priority theta = (1 + beta*w)/C reduces to a waiting-time-vs-cost density with an aging boost; the 'jointly consider throughput and delay' framing oversells what is a fairly standard heuristic.

Headline gains (6.5x/4.7x, 95-96% TTFT reduction) are largely measured at saturation points where FCFS baselines collapse; per-request efficiency gains at moderate load are much smaller (e.g., Table 7), and the paper does not clearly separate saturation-regime effects from intrinsic scheduling improvements.

Prediction quality is modest (65% bucket accuracy on INFERCEPT, MSE ~5s for call duration), and while robustness is shown empirically, there is no analysis of when mispredictions plus greedy aging can cause starvation or SLO violations for long-waiting requests.

No comparison with orthogonal augmented-serving approaches (e.g., asynchronous function calling of Gim et al., which is cited) and no statement about code/data release, which limits reproducibility of a system paper; several experimental details (e.g., exact beta_low/beta_high, training data for the BERT predictor, baseline tuning) are not fully specified.

Greedy packing breaks on the first non-fitting request (Algorithm 1, Line 38), which can under-fill the batch when requests have heterogeneous memory footprints; no analysis or empirical justification is given for this design choice versus best-fit scanning.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: serving tool-call-augmented LLM workloads, where Head-of-Line blocking and paused-request memory management genuinely degrade SLO attainment and goodput.
The motivation is well-grounded in measurements (Figures 2–5, Table 1) that concretely demonstrate the failure modes of FCFS/SJF scheduling and fixed token budgets in augmented workloads.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-3-70B), multiple GPUs (RTX 4090, H800, A100s), two datasets, two workload generators, ablation (Table 2), sensitivity to β, bursty arrivals, prediction-error injection (Figure 8), scheduling overhead, tail latency, SLO attainment, memory occupancy, and a comparison against MARS (D.6).

The state-aware space-time cost model with pre-invocation estimation and post-invocation feedback refinement is a sensible design, and the robustness analysis (Figure 8) provides evidence that mispredictions are tolerable.

Honest scoping of the theoretical contribution (Appendix E): the 1/2-approximation is clearly bounded to the simplified per-iteration knapsack subproblem, and the discussion acknowledges it does not extend to the full online problem.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is largely an incremental composition of known techniques—value-density greedy packing, SJF-style aging, output-length prediction (which itself builds on prior work), and a dynamic token budget based on free memory. Critically, the context-handling policy selection and memory-waste formulations (Appendix B, Equations 12–15) are adopted directly from INFERCEPT with little modification, so the core contribution reduces to scheduling on top of INFERCEPT's policy mechanism.

The headline claim of 4.7× improvement over INFERCEPT sits uneasily with the ablation: over the INFERCEPT baseline, +B alone yields only 41.5% goodput gain and +S (scheduling alone) reduces TTFT to 14.53s but the composite gain in goodput (0.15→1.07) conflates both components; the paper does not cleanly reconcile the geometric-mean claims with these local settings.

Baseline fairness concerns: vLLM discards KV cache on external calls by design, so the 6.5× improvement over vLLM is unsurprising and inflates the headline numbers; the most meaningful comparison is against INFERCEPT and MARS, where gains are considerably smaller. The MARS comparison is also a re-implementation of the authors' design rather than the original system.

Reproducibility is under-specified: no code or artifact release is mentioned; training details for the BERT-based predictor (only 65% bucket accuracy on INFERCEPT), the Wastep selection, and the choice of β = 5×10⁻⁵ across all settings are given only thinly. The claim that β is workload-insensitive is based on a single model/dataset/GPU combination.

Several evaluation choices are opaque: the SLO definition of 'normalized latency < 10× single-iteration time' is ambiguous; the token-budget clip parameters (βlow, βhigh, Tmax) are never given values; and it is unclear whether the predictor is trained on the same workload traces used in evaluation, which could leak distributional knowledge into scheduling.

The scheduling-value formulation (Equation 2) is heuristic; the aging term is justified as 'starvation prevention' but no starvation analysis or SLO-violation tail results for aged long requests are shown beyond P95 plots.

Presentation is dense: notation-heavy formulations (Sections 4–5, Appendices B and A) repeat the motivation text of Section 3 nearly verbatim, and the two challenges/opportunities framing adds length without additional insight.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: scheduling for augmented (tool-calling) LLM inference, where prior work (vLLM, INFERCEPT) either discards context or uses FCFS and suffers HoL blocking. The motivation is well-supported with empirical measurements (Figures 2-5, Table 1) that clearly identify two concrete limitations of existing systems.

The design is well-motivated and technically coherent: a space-time cost model that unifies prefill, decode, tool-wait, and resumption stages across context-handling policies, combined with value-density greedy scheduling and a dynamic token budget that accounts for reclaimable memory from paused requests. The formalization in Section 4 makes the problem concrete.

The evaluation is extensive and above the bar for systems papers: three GPU platforms and four models (including Llama-3-70B on multi-GPU), two datasets, two workload generators (Poisson and Gamma/bursty), a component-wise ablation (Table 2), latency breakdown (Figure 9), prediction-error robustness injection (Figure 8), per-iteration scheduling overhead measurements (Tables 3 and 6), tail-latency, SLO attainment, memory occupancy analysis, and a comparison against the closest related scheduler MARS (D.6). The ablation credibly shows state-aware scheduling is the dominant contributor (+S: 4.2x goodput) with the token budget providing complementary gains.

The paper is honest about limitations: the 1/2-approximation guarantee is explicitly scoped to a simplified per-iteration knapsack subproblem with an honest discussion that it does not extend to the full online problem; prediction accuracy (65% bucket accuracy on INFERCEPT) is reported transparently; beta sensitivity is analyzed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not adequately addressed: there is no statement about releasing code, the prediction models, or the workload traces. The system's behavior depends on several tuned components (beta, beta_low/beta_high clipping bounds, bucket sizes, BERT fine-tuning details), and without artifacts it will be hard for others to verify the large claimed gains (6.5x/4.7x).

The contribution is an integration of known techniques (SJF-style prioritization, value-density greedy knapsack, aging for starvation, adaptive batching) applied to the augmented-LLM setting. The novelty lies mainly in the state-aware cost model and cross-round feedback refinement; the core scheduling machinery is standard, and the theoretical analysis is limited to the simplified subproblem.

The gain magnitudes deserve scrutiny: vLLM's near-zero goodput under load (treating tool calls as termination) is somewhat of a strawman, and the reported 95-96% TTFT reductions largely reflect how catastrophically FCFS fails under this workload rather than a tight baseline comparison. The most informative comparisons are against SSJF (1.9x) and MARS (3.07x), where the margin is smaller, and the MARS comparison relies on the authors' own re-implementation of MARS's policy rather than its original prediction stack.

The evaluation is confined to two tool-calling datasets (INFERCEPT, ToolBench) and relatively older models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, with Llama-3-70B only in the appendix); runs are 30 minutes, so long-horizon effects, adversarial workloads, and modern function-calling agents (e.g., BFCL-style workloads, which the paper itself cites) are untested. Prediction quality degrades substantially on INFERCEPT (65%), and it is unclear how the approach transfers to workloads with even less predictable tool behavior.

Several design details are under-specified or weakly justified: the instantaneous-memory cost m_i(t) in Equation 5 is difficult to realize exactly for a paused request in practice; the bounded budget adjustment parameters (beta_low, beta_high) and the waste formulations in Appendix B are inherited from INFERCEPT with limited independent validation; and contention effects in Equations 13-14 involve approximations (L_other, N_max_fwd) whose sensitivity is not analyzed.
